title: Selling Trust From Orbit
gist: AEI's Brady Africk argues that with more than 16,000 satellites in orbit and AI making convincing fakes trivial, government shutter control over commercial satellite imagery is dead and the Earth-observation market's next differentiator is trust: customer vetting, ethics screening, and visible anti-fraud enforcement. Providers that build know-your-customer processes (Planet Labs, Vantor) keep access flowing during conflicts, while indiscriminate sellers can only shut off entirely.

insights.claim: Active satellites in orbit have grown from 848 in 2000 to more than 16,000 today, with thousands dedicated to Earth observation, collapsing imagery from a government monopoly into a commodity market.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Supply-side commoditization means Earth-observation revenue will not come from access scarcity; screen space-data names on differentiation, not constellation size.
insights.quote: According to the American Enterprise Institute’s Space Data Navigator, there were 848 active satellites in the year 2000. There are more than 16,000 today.
insights.locator: Earth observation was once the exclusive

insights.claim: Earth-observation satellites have shrunk from multibillion-dollar bus-sized spy platforms to shoebox-scale hardware that companies rather than states can launch, structurally lowering barriers to entry.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Falling capex per asset invites continued new entrants and price erosion in raw imagery; margin has to migrate to analytics and assurance.
insights.quote: Now, these satellites can be as small as a shoebox and launched by companies, not just countries.
insights.locator: Earth observation was once the exclusive

insights.claim: Imagery abundance has become a two-way accountability tool: governments use commercial images for public relations while the public independently fact-checks government claims with the same feeds.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Open-source verification is now a structural feature of geopolitical news flow — expect faster market reaction to conflict claims that can be checked from orbit.
insights.quote: Commercial providers are so plentiful that governments can leverage satellite imagery as a public relations tool, and, in turn, the public can often check a government’s claims independently.
insights.locator: Among many uses, imagery has become

insights.claim: Iran monitored U.S. troops at Al Asad Air Base in Iraq before its 2020 strike using nothing more than a commercial imagery vendor, showing adversaries need no sovereign satellite capability to build targeting-grade awareness.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Force-protection risk from commercial imagery is a live policy trigger — regulatory intervention risk sits on U.S. imagery vendors' revenue.
insights.quote: Iran needed no satellite of its own to monitor U.S. troops at Al Asad Air Base in Iraq before striking it in 2020, just a vendor with imagery to sell.
insights.locator: But that same abundance creates new risks

insights.claim: Firms that own no satellites at all, such as China's MizarVision, can still publish annotated imagery of U.S. military assets, meaning controls aimed at satellite operators miss the reseller layer.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Sanctions targeting hardware operators are structurally leaky; asset-light imagery brokers are the harder-to-regulate node in the chain.
insights.quote: Even firms like China’s MizarVision, which don’t own any satellites, can still publish annotated images of U.S. military assets.
insights.locator: But that same abundance creates new risks

insights.claim: Sanctioning the buyers of Western satellite imagery does not cut off their access because straw purchasers can conceal the ultimate end user.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Entity-list style remedies underdeliver here; the enforceable control point is customer identity verification at the vendor, not the buyer list.
insights.quote: As a result, sanctioning the firms or countries that buy satellite imagery products from Western providers will not cut off access to these images.
insights.locator: If commercial providers and vendors block sales

insights.claim: When U.S. strikes on Iran began in 2026, Washington asked American imagery providers to stop selling photos of the region and many curbed sales — including some that said they never received a request — but European and Chinese suppliers kept selling into the gap.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Voluntary U.S. blackouts transfer conflict-period imagery revenue to European and Chinese competitors — a direct share-loss mechanism during the highest-demand windows.
insights.quote: But that didn’t stop European and Chinese sources, which kept selling.
insights.locator: When strikes on Iran began in 2026

insights.claim: Some Chinese imagery firms now advertise their U.S. sanctions status as a marketing asset, inverting the intended deterrent effect of designation.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Designation is becoming a positive brand signal in non-aligned markets — a sign U.S. economic statecraft is losing bite in dual-use data.
insights.quote: Now, some Chinese imagery firms proudly brag about being under U.S. sanctions as a publicity tool.
insights.locator: Government-requested imagery blackouts create a void

insights.claim: The era in which the U.S. government could impose shutter control through legal restrictions or exclusive purchases of imagery is over, so militaries must now plan and operate on the assumption of permanent observation.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Persistent transparency raises the value of concealment, deception and mobility in defense procurement, and lowers the strategic value of static basing.
insights.quote: today’s proliferated imagery space means the world’s militaries must plan, act, and operate as if they are under observation.
insights.locator: Cutting off access was once a feasible

insights.claim: Google Earth briefly shipped a feature letting users AI-manipulate satellite images grounded in real terrain and pulled it in under a day after backlash, showing how fast mainstream tools can mass-produce geospatial misinformation absent guardrails.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Platform-level generative features are a tail risk for the credibility of all geospatial evidence; watch provenance and watermarking standards emerge as a product category.
insights.quote: For a brief window last week, the world’s most popular digital globe, Google Earth, let users manipulate satellite images with AI to create fakes grounded in real terrain.
insights.locator: High-resolution satellite imagery has never been easier

insights.claim: State actors have already weaponized doctored satellite imagery — Russia used deceptive images to deny responsibility for shooting down MH17 over Ukraine in 2014 — and AI now makes comparable fakes cheap and high-quality.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Falling cost of credible geospatial forgery raises the premium on verified-provenance imagery and on providers with authentication track records.
insights.quote: When Russia denied its role in shooting down MH17 over Ukraine in 2014, it used deceptive satellite images to further its false claims.
insights.locator: Disinformation compounds the complexity of this space

insights.claim: Fakes damage every imagery provider by degrading trust in the category as a whole, leaving companies squeezed between collapsing public credibility and government restriction.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: A classic negative-externality market — expect industry-level standards bodies or consortium verification to emerge as the rational response.
insights.quote: As a result, commercial providers face collapsing trust from the public on one side and government restrictions on the other.
insights.locator: Deceptions like these ultimately harm all imagery

insights.claim: Recency, not resolution, is what makes imagery militarily sensitive: an old image of an air base serves research while this morning's image serves targeting, implying access should be tiered by freshness rather than pixel size.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: A latency-tiered pricing and compliance model is the natural product architecture — archival open, fresh tasking gated behind KYC.
insights.quote: When it comes to satellite images, timing can matter more than resolution.
insights.locator: As a first step, more companies should engage

insights.claim: Sensitive imagery — recent high-resolution frames and satellite tasking in conflict zones — should sit behind identity confirmation and end-use scrutiny modeled on how financial institutions know their customers.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Imports a banking-style compliance cost structure into space data — a moat for scaled incumbents and a burden on small resellers.
insights.quote: More sensitive data, like recent high-resolution imagery and satellite tasking in conflict zones, should rest behind vetting that confirms a customer’s identity and scrutinizes end use, similar to how many financial institutions know their customers.
insights.locator: More sensitive data, like recent high-resolution

insights.claim: Planet Labs responded to the U.S. blackout request during the Iran war by implementing a more selective distribution model that kept urgent use cases supplied, an option only available to a provider that knows its customers.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Customer vetting is revenue insurance: it converts a total shutdown into a partial one during conflict, the highest-demand period.
insights.quote: A provider that knows its customers can do this, whereas one that sells indiscriminately can only shut off access completely to comply.
insights.locator: After American provider Planet Labs received a request

insights.claim: Providers should run public misuse-reporting portals so customers and even ordinary social media users can flag suspect content, letting firms cut off access or refute deceptions faster.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Low-cost trust infrastructure that doubles as a marketing asset — cheap differentiation for a provider chasing institutional accounts.
insights.quote: A dedicated portal through which customers, and even regular social media users, can submit suspect content will help providers cut off access or publicly refute deceptions with greater speed.
insights.locator: In addition to vetting, providers can do better

insights.claim: Executives are reluctant to publicize misuse of their imagery, but bad actors and AI fakes will surface that awareness regardless, making proactive disclosure the dominant strategy.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: First movers on transparency capture the reputational premium before the issue becomes a forced disclosure event.
insights.quote: But the reality is that deliberate misuse by bad actors and AI-fueled imagery fakes are set to bring that awareness to the public anyway.
insights.locator: Executives at commercial imagery companies could be reticent

insights.claim: Best-practice vetting exists but is not the industry norm — Planet Labs screens prospective customers and runs an ethics committee, and Vantor supplies imagery and analysis to thousands of journalists — while the broader market rewards removing barriers to access and treats end-use monitoring as discretionary.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: The gap between best practice and market reward is the arbitrage: firms investing in trust today are underpriced relative to a market that will reprice it.
insights.quote: The industry’s incentive structure today often rewards removing as many barriers to access as possible, and monitoring end use is discretionary. These tendencies sacrifice long-term trust for short-term sales.
insights.locator: Leading satellite image providers already take many

insights.claim: As the imagery market matures, providers seen as responsible and authentic will out-compete rivals, while laggards risk having their products restricted by blackouts or tainted by irresponsible use.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Frame Earth-observation equity selection around governance and compliance quality, not just refresh rate and resolution specs.
insights.quote: the future of Earth observation belongs not to those with the best access, but to those seen as reliable.
insights.locator: As the market matures and trust gains

insights.claim: Attempts to shut down imagery access entirely are futile and would destroy public-good uses including human rights documentation, disaster response, agricultural surveying, deforestation monitoring, and sea-level tracking.
insights.speaker: Brady Africk
insights.so_what: Regulatory tail risk is bounded — a full-access ban is not a credible policy path, so downside scenarios for imagery firms are about friction, not prohibition.
insights.quote: Efforts to entirely shut down imagery access are not only futile but would also hinder uses of it that benefit the common good.
insights.locator: Deceptions like these ultimately harm all imagery
